You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 4.5 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 5.5 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 4.5 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 4.5 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.8 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 120 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 4700 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 3300 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 60 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       3.33    3.36    49.3       -      5.05  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S2       3.18     3.2    44.2       -      10.1  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S3       7.08    7.13     110   0.209      5.01  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       2.21    2.22    33.8       -      1.04  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5        3.4    3.44    83.3       -       3.5  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       2.81    2.83    28.1       -       3.6  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 4.5 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo transducer.
    *   Target: $V_{out}$ between 4.5V and 5.5V, ripple $\le$ 50mV, startup $\le$ 0.4s.
    *   Piezo Model: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30nF) and $R_{leak} = 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   Operating conditions S1-S6 (nominal, heavy load, strong excitation/light load, weak excitation, low frequency, hot/high capacitance).

    *   `p_sshi_full_bridge` (c0071) is the best so far (score 43.56).
    *   It successfully reaches $\ge 4.5\text{V}$ on all conditions.
    *   However, it exceeds $5.5\text{V}$ on S1, S2, S3, S5.
    *   It has too much ripple on S2.
    *   This suggests the SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) full-bridge topology is very efficient (too efficient in some cases), and we need a way to regulate the output voltage.

    *   The failure is `vout_max > 5.5V`.
    *   We need to clamp the output voltage to 5.5V.
    *   Standard method: Zener diode or a voltage regulator.
    *   Available components: `DZ33` is a 3.3V zener. Wait, the target is 4.5V to 5.5V. A 3.3V zener would clamp it too low.
    *   Wait, the target is $V_{avg} \ge 4.5\text{V}$. If I use a zener of 3.3V, I'll never reach 4.5V.
    *   Is there any other way to regulate?
    *   The current topology `p_sshi_full_bridge` uses a full bridge of Schottky diodes and an inductor switch.
    *   If $V_{out}$ goes too high, it means the harvested energy exceeds the load consumption.

    *   How to limit $V_{out}$ to 5.5V without a specific 5.1V or 5.6V zener?
    *   Maybe I can use a Zener as part of a divider or a different clamping circuit? No, that's complex.
    *   Wait, I can use the `DZ33` in series with another diode.
    *   `DZ33` (3.3V) + `DSCH` ($\sim 0.25\text{V}$) $\approx 3.55\text{V}$. Still too low.
    *   What about two `DZ33` in series? $3.3\text{V} + 3.3\text{V} = 6.6\text{V}$. A bit too high.
    *   What about a `DZ33` and a silicon diode `DSI` ($\sim 0.5\text{V}$)? $3.3 + 0.5 = 3.8\text{V}$. Still too low.

    *   Wait, look at the `p_sshi_full_bridge` again. It's essentially a rectifier with a boost (SSHI).
    *   The voltage on the output capacitor $C_1$ builds up.
    *   The problem is that on S3 (strong excitation, light load), it hits 15.3V.
    *   Is there a way to reduce the energy harvested when $V_{out}$ is high?
    *   The `SYNC` controller is ideal; it switches at the extrema regardless of $V_{out}$.

    *   Let's re-evaluate the components. I have `R, C, L, D (DSCH, DSI, DZ33), S, SYNC`.
    *   If I can't use a zener to clamp to 5V, maybe I can use a different topology that is naturally more limited or use the Zener to create a reference.
    *   Wait, if I use a Zener `DZ33` as a clamp on a node *before* a boost stage? No.
    *   What if I use the Zener in a way that it starts conducting and shunts current when $V_{out}$ is too high?
    *   If I put a Zener from `out` to ground, it clamps to its breakdown voltage. `DZ33` clamps to 3.3V. This is below the 4.5V minimum.

    *   What if I use a different rectifier?
    *   `p_sshi_full_bridge` is:
        - D1: pzp -> out
        - D2: pzn -> out
        - D3: 0 -> pzp
        - D4: 0 -> pzn
        - L1: pzp -> n1
        - S1: n1 -> pzn
    *   This is a standard SSHI circuit. The voltage $V_{out}$ can grow quite high because the inductor flips the voltage on $C_p$, effectively adding to the charge each cycle.
    *   To limit $V_{out}$, I can:
        1.  Increase the load (not allowed, RL is fixed).
        2.  Decrease the efficiency (e.g., using a resistor in series, but that hurts startup and $V_{min}$).
        3.  Use a shunt regulator.
        4.  Change the switching timing (`ton` or `phase`)? No, that's handled by the evolution strategy.
        5.  Change the topology to one that has a natural limit.

    *   Is there a topology that limits voltage?
    *   A simple full-bridge rectifier (FBR) without SSHI: $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} + V_{out} - 2V_d$? No, $V_{out}$ usually settles around $V_{oc} - 2V_d$ if not boosted. In the reference FBR, $V_{out}$ was 3.33V (S1), which is below 4.5V. So SSHI is necessary to get above 4.5V.

    *   How to clamp to 5.5V?
    *   If I use two `DZ33` in series: $3.3 + 3.3 = 6.6\text{V}$.
    *   If I use one `DZ33` and one `DSI` and one `DSCH`? $3.3 + 0.5 + 0.25 = 4.05\text{V}$.
    *   What if I use a `DZ33` and another `DZ33` in a specific configuration?
    *   Wait, the `DZ33` is a 3.3V Zener. If I put it in series with something that has a voltage drop... but Zener breakdown is the point where it conducts.
    *   If I put two `DZ33` in series (cathodes to anodes), they block. If I put them in series (anode to cathode, cathode to anode... no).
    *   If I put them as: `out` -> `DZ33(cathode)` -> `DZ33(anode)` -> `DZ33(cathode)` -> `0`.
    *   Then $V_{out}$ would be clamped at $3.3\text{V} + 3.3\text{V} = 6.6\text{V}$. Still too high.

    *   Let's look at the failure on S3: $V_{out} = 15.3\text{V}$. This is much higher than 5.5V.
    *   S1: 6.94V. S2: 6.26V. S5: 7.42V.
    *   All these are only slightly above 5.5V, except S3.
    *   Maybe I can use a larger storage capacitor $C_1$ to reduce ripple, but $V_{max}$ is the main issue.

    *   Is there a way to use the inductor to regulate?
    *   In SSHI, the amount of charge transferred depends on $L$ and $t_{on}$.
    *   If $L$ is smaller, less charge is transferred?
    *   Wait, if I use a *different* rectifier?
    *   What about a charge pump?
    *   Or a "Half-Bridge" SSHI? The `p_sshi_half_bridge` failed miserably because $V_{out}$ went negative or didn't reach 4.5V.

    *   Let's try to add a "bleeder" or "clamp" that only activates at high voltages.
    *   Since I only have `DZ33`, maybe I can use a `DZ33` and a `DSI` in some way?
    *   Wait, what if I use the `DZ33` to clamp the piezo voltage *before* it reaches the rectifier?
    *   If I put a `DZ33` from `pzp` to `pzn`, it will clamp the piezo voltage to $3.3\text{V} \times 2 = 6.6\text{V}$ (peak-to-peak).
    *   The open circuit voltage is $3.8\text{V}$ peak ($7.6\text{V}$ pk-pk).
    *   Clamping the piezo voltage might reduce the energy harvested, but it might also limit the output voltage.
    *   Let's try: `DZ33` from `pzp` to `pzn` (and maybe another one in reverse?).
    *   Actually, a simpler clamp: `DZ33` from `out` to `0` is 3.3V.
    *   Wait, if I use a `DZ33` and a `DSI` and a `DSCH` in series?
    *   Anode `DSI` at `out`, cathode `DSI` to anode `DSCH`, cathode `DSCH` to cathode `DZ33`, anode `DZ33` to `0`.
    *   This would be: $V_{out} = V_{DSI} + V_{DSCH} + V_{Zener} = 0.5 + 0.25 + 3.3 = 4.05\text{V}$. Still too low.
    *   What if I use two `DSI` and one `DZ33`? $0.5 + 0.5 + 3.3 = 4.3\text{V}$.
    *   What if I use three `DSI` and one `DZ33`? $0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 3.3 = 4.8\text{V}$.
    *   This could be a clamp!
    *   Clamp: `out` -> `DSI` -> `DSI` -> `DSI` -> `DZ33` -> `0` (with `DZ33` cathode at the top).
    *   Wait, Zener `DZ33` orientation: "reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above".
    *   So for `DZ33`, cathode is at the higher potential.
    *   Clamp: `out` (node A) -> `S_diode` (cathode) -> `S_diode` (anode) ... no.
    *   Correct sequence: `out` -> `cathode DZ33`, `anode DZ33` -> `cathode DSI`, `anode DSI` -> `cathode DSI`, `anode DSI` -> `0`.
    *   Wait, `DSI` is a regular diode. It only conducts in one direction.
    *   For the clamp to work, the current must flow from `out` to `0`.
    *   So: `out` -> `cathode DZ33`, `anode DZ33` -> `anode DSI`, `cathode DSI` -> `0`.
    *   Wait, `anode DSI` to `cathode DSI` is forward bias.
    *   So: `out` -> `cathode DZ33` -> `anode DZ33` -> `anode DSI` -> `cathode DSI` -> `0`.
    *   Voltage at which it conducts: $V_{DZ33} + V_{DSI} = 3.3 + 0.5 = 3.8\text{V}$.
    *   If I use three `DSI`: $3.3 + 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 4.8\text{V}$.
    *   If I use two `DSI`: $3.3 + 0.5 + 0.5 = 4.3\text{V}$.
